_disclaimer: Illustrative mock data built for a demonstration. The episodes referenced are real, but every figure here is fabricated and rounded for teaching purposes. Nothing here is research, and past behaviour of other investors is not a prediction of any future outcome.

aggregate.description: Mock cohort of retail accounts that liquidated 50%+ of equity holdings within 5 trading days of a >3% single-day drawdown.
aggregate.plain_language: In this mock cohort, about 2 in 3 investors who sold during the drop bought back in at a higher price than they sold at.

cases.panic_seller_outcome: Sold near the bottom and, on average in this mock cohort, re-entered 23% higher.
cases.stayed_invested_outcome: Recovered the full drawdown within roughly 5 months without acting.

cases.panic_seller_outcome: Exited growth and tech positions mid-decline; missed the subsequent recovery leg in this mock cohort.
cases.stayed_invested_outcome: Flat-to-down for roughly 9 months, then fully recovered.

cases.panic_seller_outcome: Sold during a three-day scare; the index reclaimed the level inside a month.
cases.stayed_invested_outcome: Round-tripped the move with no action taken.

cases.panic_seller_outcome: Roughly half of this mock cohort avoided further downside — the fundamentals really had changed.
cases.stayed_invested_outcome: Mixed. Recovery was slower and less reliable than after broad market dips.
cases.note: Important counterweight: when the news is genuinely company-specific, selling has historically been a far more defensible decision than when the move is market-wide. The distinction matters more than the emotion.

aggregate.description: Mock cohort of retail accounts that opened a new position in a name after it had already risen 100%+ within 90 days.
aggregate.plain_language: In this mock cohort, roughly 7 in 10 of these entries were underwater three months later, and most were sold within a month.

cases.late_buyer_outcome: Entries made in the final week of the run-up were down sharply within a month in this mock cohort.
Sector-level entries near the peak took over two years to recover, and many names never did.
Volatile, and drawdowns were severe mid-run — but this cohort was net positive at 12 months.
cases.note: Counterweight: not every crowded trade ends badly. Some run-ups are backed by real and growing earnings. The question worth asking is which kind this one is.

aggregate.description: Mock cohort of retail accounts whose trade was placed within 48h of a widely-shared social or peer signal, with no stated personal reason.
aggregate.plain_language: In this mock cohort, roughly 2 in 3 of these copied trades left the account worse off at 12 months than doing nothing would have.

cases.case: Copying a widely-shared 'I sold everything' post
cases.outcome: The poster's situation — time horizon, tax position, concentration, whether they needed the cash — was almost never the same as the follower's.
Institutional disclosures lag by weeks. In this mock cohort the move was largely priced in before retail followers could act.

cases.case: Peer or group-chat driven entry into a single name
cases.outcome: Concentration rose without any change to the follower's actual plan; position sizing was copied from someone with a different portfolio size.
